questions.q: Why does a trapped-ion qubit use a charged ion rather than a neutral atom?
options: A charged particle can be confined by electric and electromagnetic fields, which is how the Paul trap holds it in place; a neutral atom can't be grabbed this way
Charged ions naturally emit the laser light needed for cooling, so no laser is required
Charge has no role in trapping; it only affects the ion's color
Neutral atoms are too large to fit inside a vacuum chamber
questions.explain: Electrostatics forbids trapping a charged particle with static fields alone, but a Paul trap's oscillating RF field (plus static fields) can confine a charged ion in a stable region of space -- this only works because the ion carries a net charge.

questions.q: Where is the quantum information (the |0> and |1> states) physically encoded in a trapped-ion qubit?
options: In the physical position of the ion along the trap's axis
In the voltage applied to the trap's electrodes at any given moment
In two long-lived internal electronic/hyperfine energy levels of the ion itself
In the color of the vacuum chamber's glass
questions.explain: The qubit states are two internal energy levels of the ion (often hyperfine or optical 'clock' states) chosen because they're long-lived and relatively insensitive to stray fields -- not the ion's position or the trap hardware.

questions.q: When several ions are loaded into the same linear trap, what causes them to settle into an evenly spaced chain rather than clumping together?
options: Each ion is cooled to a different temperature, which keeps them apart
The ions are physically glued to fixed positions on a substrate
Mutual Coulomb repulsion between the identically charged ions balances against the trap's confining force
The laser beams used for cooling physically push the ions apart
questions.explain: All the ions carry the same positive charge, so they repel each other; the balance between that repulsion and the trap's confinement is what produces the stable, evenly spaced chain.

questions.q: Why is laser (Doppler) cooling a required step before running gates on a trapped-ion chain, not an optional optimization?
options: Cooling permanently changes which element the ion is made of
Lasers are only needed to make the ions visible for photographs, not for any physics reason
Freshly loaded ions have energetic, effectively random motion, and gates require the chain's motion to be quiet and well-controlled -- close to the motional ground state
Cooling is only done for aesthetic reasons and has no effect on gate performance
questions.explain: Gate operations rely on controlled interactions with the ion's motion; an ion chain that starts out thermally 'hot' has to be cooled, typically via Doppler cooling, toward its motional ground state before reliable gates are possible.

questions.q: What is one practical advantage trapped-ion qubits have over superconducting qubits purely because of how they're created?
options: Trapped ions never need to be cooled before use
Every ion of a given element is naturally identical to every other one, avoiding the chip-to-chip fabrication variation superconducting qubits must contend with
Trapped ions can be created at room temperature with no vacuum chamber required
Trapped-ion gates are always faster than superconducting gates
questions.explain: Because trapped-ion qubits are naturally occurring atoms rather than lithographically fabricated circuits, they don't suffer from the manufacturing-variation problem that affects superconducting qubits -- though they introduce their own engineering challenges, like needing lasers and vacuum systems.
